Projeto "Defensoria Tá na Área" — Foto: Divulgação/DPE-AM

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

A Defensoria Pública do Amazonas (DPAM) oferece 520 vagas para atendimento jurídico gratuito neste sábado (28), das 8h às 15h, no Mercado de Origem, localizado na Rua Tamandaré, 22, no Centro Histórico de Manaus . Os atendimentos serão nas áreas de Família e Direito do Consumidor.

Os agendamentos devem ser feitos antecipadamente pelos canais oficiais da Defensoria. No momento da marcação, os interessados recebem orientações sobre os documentos necessários para cada tipo de atendimento.

Telefones: (92) 3198-1200 e (92) 3198-1300;

Do total de vagas, 420 são destinadas a demandas da área de Família e 100 a casos relacionados ao Direito do Consumidor.

Esta edição do projeto "Defensoria Tá na Área" terá, pela primeira vez, a participação do Núcleo de Defesa do Consumidor (Nudecon). O setor vai atender pessoas com problemas como cobranças indevidas, golpes envolvendo empréstimos, dificuldades com serviços de telefonia e dívidas acumuladas.

Na área de Família, serão oferecidas orientações e assistência jurídica em casos de pensão alimentícia, guarda de filhos, divórcio e reconhecimento ou dissolução de união estável.

Criado em março de 2025, o projeto busca levar os serviços da Defensoria a diferentes regiões de Manaus e facilitar o acesso da população à assistência jurídica gratuita.

articles.title: Lula inspira esquerda na Espanha e recebe críticas da direita  | G1
articles.standfirst: Lula acabou se tornando personagem das eleições na Espanha em 29 de novembro, onde os favoritos são o atual premiê, Pedro Sánchez, do Partido Socialista Operário Espanhol, de esquerda, e Alberto Núñez Feijóo, do Partido Popular, de direita.
articles.summary: Lula acabou se tornando personagem das eleições na Espanha em 29 de novembro, onde os favoritos são o atual premiê, Pedro Sánchez, de esquerda, e Alberto Núñez Feijóo, de direita.
articles.body:
Em 16 de novembro, Lula desembarcou em Madri acompanhado do deputado André Janones, na volta de uma viagem à Ásia, para manifestar seu apoio a Sánchez na reta final da campanha espanhola. — Foto: EPA/ Shutterstock via BBC

Adicione o g1 como Fonte Preferida no Google

Em um dos vídeos mais inusitados da campanha eleitoral espanhola, o primeiro-ministro Pedro Sánchez, do Partido Socialista Operário Espanhol (PSOE), aparece como um super-herói de anime japonês . Ele enfrenta, em Madri, uma versão supervilã de seu principal adversári o nas eleições gerais de 29 de novembro: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, líder do Partido Popular (PP), de centro-direita.

Até que, em meio ao confronto, o presidente brasileiro Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) entra em cena para ajudar Sánchez, lançando para ele um chapéu que se transforma em um escudo protetor com o símbolo de uma rosa.

Com o reforço brasileiro, o socialista derrota Feijóo e sua "comparsa", uma hidra de três cabeças com os rostos do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, do presidente argentino, Javier Milei, e do primeiro-ministro israelense, Benjamin Netanyahu .

O vídeo termina com Sánchez fazendo um "L" ao lado de Lula.

Animação coloca Pedro Sánchez como herói e fazendo 'L' ao lado de Lula. — Foto: Reprodução/ André Rocha via BBC

👉 Criada pelo designer português André Rocha, autor de uma animação semelhante com Lula que viralizou no Brasil, a produção foi divulgada dias depois de o PP lançar um vídeo com a mesma estética e de ser acusado pelo jornal "El País" de ter "copiado" o original de Lula. Na produção do PP, a batalha também acontece em Madri, mas os papéis se invertem: desta vez, o supervilão é Sánchez.

Feijóo, um político de 65 anos conhecido por seu perfil austero e tecnocrático , reconheceu que nem entendeu muito bem a animação.

"Eu sou um boomer [geração nascida entre 1945 e 1965]. Não tenho vergonha nem escondo isso. Mas começo a pensar que, entre o vídeo que vocês mostraram hoje e as montagens que circulam por aí durante a campanha… isso está indo longe demais", disse o candidato, no lançamento da animação, em um evento com jovens do partido.

"Não sei se peço a vocês que me expliquem o que está acontecendo ou se é melhor nem ficar sabendo. Por enquanto, estou optando pela segunda alternativa. Mas reconheço que estou me divertindo."

Os dois vídeos mostram como Lula e sua campanha presidencial no Brasil se tornaram referências na disputa política espanhola, influenciando até a comunicação de partidos adversários.

A virada surpreendente do brasileiro no segundo turno das eleições e o papel das redes sociais na reta final de sua campanha transformaram o brasileiro em uma espécie de estudo de caso para os candidatos espanhóis , que se enfrentam em uma disputa também marcada pela polarização.

Um dia depois da vitória de Lula, o portal "Metrópoles" divulgou que o deputado federal André Janones (Rede-MG), responsável pela estratégia digital que contribuiu para a vitória do petista, foi "convidado a ajudar" na campanha de Sánchez.

Em 16 de novembro, Lula desembarcou em Madri acompanhado de Janones , na volta de uma viagem à Ásia, para manifestar seu apoio a Sánchez na reta final da campanha espanhola.

Lula e Sánchez discutiram, segundo o Palácio da Moncloa, a sede do governo em Madri, "o futuro das Nações Unidas e a importância de se defender as instituições democráticas e a coesão social diante das ameaças da ultradireita".

A participação do líder brasileiro em um ato de campanha acabou sendo cancelada porque Lula estaria sem voz. No dia seguinte, porém, Sánchez chamou Lula de "ciclone" durante um comício e disse que usava "com orgulho" uma camisa autografada pelo brasileiro.

Janones publicou em seu canal do WhatsApp "Exército de Lula" uma foto ao lado de Aránzazu Figueroa, responsável pela estratégia digital do PSOE.

Em entrevista ao jornal digital "El Español", o deputado afirmou que sua colaboração com a equipe de Sánchez incluiu gravações, orientações e sugestões, mas minimizou seu envolvimento na campanha: "Aceitei o convite para ajudar de alguma maneira, mas de forma sutil, para que não seja confundido com uma interferência brasileira nas eleições espanholas."

A mensagem foi repetida em entrevista ao "El País" no domingo.

"Compartilhei com eles [lideranças do PSOE] nossa experiência, dei algumas recomendações e conversei com a jovem responsável pelo canal [Figueroa]. Mas não participo diretamente da campanha de Sánchez", disse Janones. "Estou sob a liderança de Lula. E ele, como estadista que é, não interfere nas eleições de outros países."

Tanto o governo espanhol quanto o PSOE negam que Janones esteja assessorando formalmente a campanha de Sánchez ou que haja planos para isso. A justificativa é que a estratégia digital socialista já vinha sendo desenvolvida há muito tempo e segue uma linha diferente daquela adotada pelo brasileiro.

Ainda assim, chamam a atenção algumas semelhanças. Por exemplo, uma das iniciativas da campanha de Sánchez foi a criação do canal de WhatsApp "La Fuerza de la Gente", administrado por Figueroa, que publica conteúdos para mobilizar apoiadores do PSOE.

Algumas mensagens lembram a dinâmica do "Exército de Lula", como orientações aos seguidores para ajudar o canal a crescer e uma lista de regras para neutralizar "o algoritmo dos ultras ["ultradireitistas"]" e "deixar a extrema direita sem oxigênio".

A iniciativa espanhola, porém, tinha cerca de 91 mil seguidores até terça-feira (24), contra os mais de 10 milhões alcançados por Janones durante a campanha.

As limitações para 'fórmula' da esquerda brasileira na Espanha

TV em bar em Madri mostra debate entre Pedro Sánchez e Alberto Núñez Feijóo em debate; sucesso da campanha de Lula está influenciando comunicação de partidos adversários. — Foto: Reuters via BBC

O próprio Janones reconheceu limites à aplicação da estratégia brasileira ao estimar, na entrevista ao "El País", que apenas "entre 50% e 60%" dessa estratégia poderia ser reproduzida nas eleições espanholas.

Uma das razões seria que poucos países superam o Brasil em tempo diário de navegação na internet. De fato, segundo o relatório Digital 2025, da We Are Social e Meltwater, os brasileiros passam, em média, 3h32 por dia nas redes sociais, contra 1h55 dos espanhóis — ou seja, 84% a mais.

Para Susanne Gratius, professora de Relações Internacionais da Universidade Autônoma de Madri (UAM) e pesquisadora associada do CIDOB (Barcelona Centre for International Affairs), outros fatores limitam a adoção da estratégia de Lula na Espanha.

"Para começar, enquanto Lula tinha pouca presença nas redes sociais, Sánchez já é muito ativo. Além disso, a polarização política espanhola não é comparável à brasileira, já que a maioria dos eleitores têm posições mais moderadas," explica Gratius.

Ela observa que Feijóo também é mais moderado que Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) , derrotado por Lula no segundo turno.

E o sistema político espanhol é diferente . Enquanto o Brasil é uma república presidencialista, com eleições em dois turnos, que frequentemente culminam em uma votação entre apenas dois candidatos, a Espanha é uma monarquia parlamentarista .

Na prática, os eleitores escolhem em um turno deputados que, por sua vez, elegem o chefe de governo. A cada eleição geral, há múltiplas opções nas urnas.

Segundo as pesquisas, o cenário mais provável para o resultado da eleição do dia 29 é a vitória de uma coalizão de direita liderada pelo PP, com possível participação do Vox, partido de direita radical e forte viés anti-imigração.

👉 Pelo agregador de pesquisas do "El País", por exemplo, o PP teria 31,4% das intenções de voto, contra 29,1% do PSOE e 17,9% do Vox . Somando 1,8% de outro partido (o Se Acabó La Fiesta, SALF), o bloco da direita chegaria a 51,1%, contra 38,7% da esquerda.

A pesquisa 40dB, também para o "El País", projeta que, juntos, PP e Vox poderiam conseguir cerca de 187 das 350 cadeiras do Congresso, o que seria suficiente para formar governo.

"A situação seria mais semelhante [à brasileira] se a disputa fosse apenas entre Sánchez e Santiago Abascal [líder do Vox], por exemplo," diz Gratius.

Para José Javier Olivas Osuna, professor de Ciência Política da Universidade Nacional de Educação a Distância (UNED) e pesquisador associado da London School of Economics (LSE), não surpreende que o PP tenha lançado sua versão do vídeo em estilo anime antes do PSOE:

"O PP se antecipou ao PSOE no uso de vídeos com IA [inteligência artificial] na campanha , até por sua necessidade de disputar o voto jovem com o Vox."

Em montagens nas redes sociais, Feijóo aparece como rapper, coberto de correntes, ou cantando reggaeton.

"Feijóo é um burocrata da Galícia [região que governou de 2009 a 2022], enquanto o Vox construiu uma imagem de partido irreverente, que se atreve a transgredir limites e convenções. Nesse contexto, as redes sociais têm sido um instrumento importante para o PP tentar rejuvenescer a imagem de seu candidato," comenta Olivas.

Reações ao papel de Lula na eleição espanhola

Sánchez tem mencionado a vitória de Lula como prova de que ainda é possível reverter as pesquisas desfavoráveis.

"A virada épica que você conseguiu no Brasil me leva a uma conclusão: quando a esquerda acredita na vitória — apesar das análises e pesquisas desfavoráveis —, acaba conquistando essa vitória," disse o primeiro-ministro espanhol ao brasileiro durante a visita, como mostra um vídeo divulgado pelo PSOE.

A proximidade entre os dois líderes também tem provocado reações na oposição espanhola. O próprio Feijóo criticou o primeiro-ministro espanhol por, supostamente, gastar muito tempo com o Brasil.

"[Precisamos de] menos olhar para fora e mais cuidar dos problemas da Espanha. Menos olhar para o Brasil e mais olhar para como encher a geladeira com alimentos básicos", disse o líder do PP dias antes da chegada de Lula.

Isabel Díaz Ayuso, governadora da Comunidade de Madri, também do PP, associou a presença de Lula a "forças externas" que tentariam influenciar as eleições.

"[Essas] são eleições fundamentais para a Europa e especialmente para o continente americano, porque todo o mundo hispânico está agora de olho nessas eleições. Há cada vez mais forças externas — por exemplo, agora com a presença de Lula", afirmou à emissora argentina Radio Mitre.

Lula e Sánchez estreitaram seus laços políticos nos últimos anos e estão entre as principais referências da esquerda internacional. O apoio de Lula à campanha do socialista espanhol, porém, levanta dúvidas sobre o futuro das relações Brasil-Espanha caso a direita vença as eleições de domingo, especialmente diante de uma possível coalizão com o Vox.

Segundo Sergio Caballero, professor de Relações Internacionais da Universidade Nebrija, uma vitória da direita não deve comprometer as relações econômicas entre Brasil e Espanha, já que os vínculos empresariais entre os dois países estão consolidados.

"Mas o mesmo não se pode dizer das relações políticas. Nos últimos anos, sob o governo Sánchez, a Espanha desempenhou um papel importante na aproximação da América Latina e do Brasil com a União Europeia, sendo uma das principais forças defensoras do acordo comercial com o Mercosul", comenta.

"Essa sintonia política e o papel da Espanha como articuladora da relação Europa-América Latina tenderiam a enfraquecer sob um governo da direita. E Feijóo também teria menor projeção internacional. É ilustrativo, por exemplo, que ao contrário de Sánchez, ele não fale inglês."

Caballero acrescenta que o eventual grau de distanciamento político entre Brasil e Espanha também dependeria do peso do Vox em uma coalizão de governo.

"O partido de Abascal poderia assumir posições mais antagônicas ao governo Lula, gerando tensões em áreas como imigração e comércio ", afirma.

Ainda assim, nenhum dos especialistas consultados pela BBC News Brasil prevê uma eventual ruptura diplomática caso a direita vença. Para Gratius, mesmo que a perspectiva de uma relação entre Abascal e Lula seja ruim, é improvável que o Vox controle a política externa espanhola.

"O PP tenderia a manter o Ministério das Relações Exteriores. Até porque as posições eurocéticas do Vox poderiam criar muitas dificuldades para o governo espanhol", completa.

articles.title: A man in Boston won $1 million in the lottery. Then ICE arrested him
articles.summary: Salvadoran national Ariel Velasquez-Morales, who ICE says was in the country illegally for more than a decade, won $1 million playing a scratch-off ticket in...
articles.body:
Over the weekend, the Massachusetts Lottery shared a picture of Ariel Velasquez-Morales smiling gently as he gripped an oversized check for $1 million in winnings. On social media, commenters congratulated him, with one person writing they hoped he would be able to "make any dreams come true."

But Velasquez-Morales was arrested Tuesday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in East Boston, the same neighborhood where he bought the $10 winning scratch-off ticket from a local market.

He now faces deportation as ICE says the Salvadoran national has been in the country illegally for more than a decade.

"Looks like his luck ran out," said ICE Assistant Director of Public Affairs Micah Bock in a release announcing the arrest.

It is unclear whether the publication of his lottery winnings attracted ICE's attention. ICE declined to answer questions from CNN about what led to the arrest or where Velasquez-Morales is being detained.

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the United States in 2013, during the Obama administration, in the Rio Grande Valley in Texas. Border Patrol agents issued him a notice to appear before an immigration judge, and he was released into the country with a list of free legal service providers, the agency said.

"A Department of Justice immigration judge ordered Velasquez-Morales removed in 2014, but he illegally remained in the country," the ICE release said.

He will remain in ICE custody pending his removal from the US. CNN has been unable to determine whether he has legal representation.

President Donald Trump has overseen a massive immigration crackdown after promising to lead the largest deportation operation in US history. In his second term, arrests have shifted away from the border and focused more on the interior of the country, where aggressive tactics have become a hallmark of ICE's ramped-up detention efforts. By July 2026, there were nearly 66,000 detainees in ICE custody, an increase of nearly 70% from the total detained when Trump took office the year prior.

But after a Republican wipeout in the midterms, Trump has publicly questioned whether the tactics were too hard-line and unpopular. It remains to be seen, though, whether he is considering significant changes to his immigration policies.

"Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the United States and will be removed as quickly as possible," ICE said in its release on Velasquez-Morales. "Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin's leadership, ICE is delivering on its mission to enforce our nation's immigration laws, restore accountability and protect American communities."

Velasquez-Morales was playing the lottery's " $2,000,000 50X Cashword ," in which players scratch cards resembling crossword puzzles to try to reveal complete words. It was the first puzzle he had scratched, the lottery said, and he matched 11 words.

He chose to accept his winnings in cash, which would give him a one-time lump sum of $650,000 before taxes, according to ICE. It is not clear what will happen to his winnings.

Massachusetts lottery participants do not need to be legal residents of the state to play, but they must be 21 or older and be located in the state at the time they purchase or play.

CNN has sought comment from the Massachusetts State Lottery Commission.

articles.title: Cambridge man 'regrets surviving' fatal e-bike fire
articles.summary: Scott Peden says he was powerless to put out the fatal fire that tore through the family's home.
articles.body:
When Scott Peden thinks of the night his family died in a fire caused by an e-bike battery, he has one overriding regret: "That I lived, and they didn't."

His girlfriend Gemma Germeney, 31, and their children Lilly, eight, and Oliver, four, died after the battery exploded in their Cambridge home on 30 June 2023.

An inquest recorded conclusions of death by misadventure .

Peden, 33, says: "If I'd known about how dangerous electric bikes were, I would have been content riding a [pedal] bike.

"And on the night the only regret is that I lived and they didn't. The only regret is buying the damn electric bike and being the only one that lived."

Describing his partner, he says she "never had a bad word to say about anyone", adding: "She was artistic, she loved to draw, she loved to colour, she had such ambition with creativity."

Lilly, he says, was "the cheekiest little girl you've ever met" while "Oliver loved his motorbikes, he loved his cars and, most of all, he loved his sister.

"They had such an amazing relationship. It's unlike any siblings I've ever seen. Most siblings argue and fight, but these two just didn't."

Peden bought the e-bike in order to travel to and from his job in retail.

It had been plugged in under the stairs to recharge.

He says the night of the fire at their Sackville Close home was "just a normal night", but about 45 minutes before his early-morning alarm for work was due to go off, the family were woken by a bang.

"It shook the house and scared everyone in it," he says.

He went out of the bedroom to see what was happening and was confronted by flames.

"The only way I could describe it is an old World War Two scene where they've got flame-throwers. It was just shooting up the stairs with such ferocity," he says.

It appeared the walls were "dripping fire" and he ran to the window to call for help.

"I looked back and Gemma was panicking trying to get the kids together and I told her I'll be right back," he said.

He jumped out of the window, went through the back door and saw the house engulfed in flames.

When he got to the bike, he says he "realised there's no way I can put this out".

He was unable to get it out of the building and even tried to kick the charger out of the wall.

But realising "there's nothing I can do", he called to Germeney to jump.

"I never heard from them again," he says.

Peden, who broke an ankle jumping from the window and also suffered burns, was placed in an induced coma for four weeks and woke to be told that his family and their two dogs had been killed.

In that moment, he says, he felt "lost".

"I'd been in a relationship with Gemma for 14 years and we were talking about marriage. She was the one."

He is still dealing with the physical effects of the fire and says: "I'm not the same person that jumped out that window. That person has died.

"The person I am now is a nerve-stricken mess. Work have to let me know every time they are doing a fire drill because if I hear a fire alarm, my heart starts jumping."

Details of support with bereavement is available at BBC Action Line .

On the purchase of the e-bike, Peden says he feels he has been "punished for three years for trying to make my life a little bit easier".

The inquest heard it had been modified and the battery was a second-hand replacement, but the coroner said there was insufficient evidence for her to find that repairs done to the battery had caused the blaze.

Prior to the inquest, Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service wrote to the coroner, requesting they push for better regulation of online sales of e-bike batteries.

Assistant chief fire officer Stuart Smith told the BBC he had the same concerns about the secondhand market in lithium ion batteries.

He said there also needed to be "a cultural change", particularly around charging phones, tablets and other devices overnight.

"The advice from us, really, is please follow the manufacturer's guidance and only use the charging device supplied with the battery," he explained.

"Make sure you are alert and awake so you are able to switch it off when it is 100% charged, and can keep an eye on the temperature, and think about where you are charging them, should something happen."

Since the fire, Peden has campaigned for tighter regulations, highlighting the death of Elisha Brabin and three of her children in Bootle, Merseyside, last month, caused by an e-scooter lithium-ion battery that was on charge at the time.

"It seems like no-one's learnt a thing in the three years since," he says.

He is fundraising to cover the cost of his legal representation at the inquest, saying: "I'm just so determined that this doesn't get swept under the rug as another tragic accident. I won't allow it. And I won't stop."

Speaking after the inquest concluded, he welcomed coroner Elizabeth Gray's request for submissions about a possible prevention of future deaths report.

"We need this... report to come out and the government and the Secretary of State [for Business] to actually pay attention this time," he said.

articles.title: Great markets ‘reflect the people who use them’
articles.summary: Successful markets are built by reflecting the people who use them, says a market chief.
articles.body:
A great market is not built with fairy lights or flashy advertising, according to the head of the UK's market industry body. It is built by reflecting the people who use it.

The comments come after the cancellation of the Kernow Christmas Market in Pool, Cornwall, following a backlash over AI-generated promotional images that visitors and traders said did not match the reality of the event.

For David Catterall, chief executive of the National Association of British Market Authorities, authenticity is the ingredient shared by successful markets across the country.

"What makes a great market is that they represent the community that they're serving," he said.

Thriving markets reflected local tastes, whether through food, drink or the balance between traditional and modern traders, said Catterall.

He said markets that became part of the fabric of their communities acted as social hubs and meeting places while also boosting the local economy.

Festive market cancels bookings after AI backlash

Concerns over security costs for Christmas markets

Christmas markets 2026: Where to go in the South West and Channel Islands

Alastair Crouchen, who runs Paignton Mushrooms and has traded at Totnes Market for about five years, said: "I come back because I've got a lot of friends in the community and long-standing customers.

"There's a good selection of traders, all selling nice stuff, a lot of it locally made," he said.

Totnes Market, along with Barnstaple, is among NABMA's top 20 UK markets in the 2027 awards.

Crouchen said one of Totnes Market's biggest strengths was the atmosphere among traders.

"There's a really good camaraderie between us traders, we all get on really well with each other," he said.

Catterall said markets were performing strongly despite challenges facing many high streets.

Shoppers, particularly younger ones, increasingly viewed markets as experiences rather than simply places to buy goods, he said.

On the controversy surrounding AI-generated marketing, Catterall said operators should always "be authentic" and accurately represent what visitors could expect.

Totnes Market appears to be doing exactly that, according to Crouchen.

The fallout from the cancelled Kernow Christmas Market is still being felt by some traders.

Steve Saints, who sells 3D-printed creations, said he had spent months preparing stock for the event and was now weighing up whether to accept an offer to trade elsewhere within the Winter Wonderland attraction.

"We're all a little bit gutted," he said.

The market's organisers have said they will refund stallholders.

Kernow Christmas Market said on Facebook the event was organised and operated by Pool Market, running alongside Cornwall Winter Wonderland.

It said: "We are a small, family run business that started many years ago here in Cornwall.

"This year, as an add on from Cornwall's Winter Wonderland we thought we would try and do a good deed and bring a little festive magic into Pool Market and for those who live locally in Cornwall.

"The agreement was always with Pool Market to do their bit and we do ours. We advertise it, book the stalls and they do the rest- such as signage, decorating and greeting the traders and helping them with queries.

"We are gutted, just as much as you all that things didn't go as planned."

It said Cornwall Winter Wonderland would remain open until 3 January.

Pool Market has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Paul Whitehouse calls on prime minister to save Windermere fish
articles.summary: The comedian warns extinction beckons for Arctic charr in Windermere after thousands of years.
articles.body:
Comedian and TV presenter Paul Whitehouse has called for the government to help save an at-risk fish species present in England's largest lake since the end of the last Ice Age.

Windermere, in the Lake District, has been home to Arctic charr for more than 10,000 years, but campaigners warn extinction beckons as the fish's habitat is harmed by sewage pollution, invasive species competing for food and rising temperatures caused by global warming.

Whitehouse urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to act and said it would be "a crime" if the species were lost.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it shared "the public's determination to protect this iconic lake".

Whitehouse, who fronts the BBC's Mortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing series alongside fellow comedian Bob Mortimer, said the "spawning grounds for this beautiful species are covered in algal sludge that is a direct result of sewage pollution".

"This government needs to act now," he added.

The former Fast Show star is helping environmental campaigner Matt Staniek unveil a 1.3m (5ft 6in) ice sculpture depicting the prime minister outside No 10 North, in Manchester, to highlight the fish's plight.

Staniek wants the prime minister to expedite a £3.7bn scheme that would include a huge tunnel carrying sewage to a new state-of-the-art water treatment works .

It has been drawn up by the Only Rainwater In Windermere coalition comprising United Utilities (UU), the Environment Agency, Lake District National Park Authority (LDNPA), the Love Windermere partnership, Save Windermere campaign group and Westmorland and Furness Council.

It comes as new research from the Freshwater Biological Association (FBA) also warns Arctic charr are in serious decline and face extinction in the lake without "urgent action".

The fish, which is genetically distinct from Arctic charr in the region's other lakes, lives in four separate populations in Windermere that spawn at different times of year and different places and do not interbreed.

The FBA said spawning habitat quality had "declined markedly" at Windermere since 2017 with levels of silt and algae increasing while introduced species, such as ruffe, roach and bream, were "on the rise".

Dr Louise Lavictoire, the organisation's head of science, said the research had "shown very clearly that we are at risk of losing Arctic charr from Windermere completely".

"The species is facing multiple pressures and research gives us the evidence, data and sense of urgency to take collective action to protect this ancient fish species before it's too late."

The research was funded by groups including Natural England, the Environment Agency and the LDNPA.

Natural England's Dave Ottewell described Arctic charr as "remarkable fish" and a "living link to the end of the last Ice Age".

Tim Duckmanton, team leader for strategy and environment at the LDNPA, echoed that sentiment and said "thanks to data collected, we now have a better understanding of threats to the species".

UU, which manages infrastructure around the lake, said protecting the area was a "priority" and that £200m was being invested over the next four years in an effort to cut spills from storm overflows and improve wastewater treatment.

A Defra spokesperson said: "This government is already acting to reduce sewage discharges, including deploying 33 additional Environment Agency specialists in the region, increasing inspections and through our regional water council's giving the local community in Windermere a greater say in decision making.

"Our strengthened Water Bill will bring in tougher regulation, stronger enforcement and greater accountability, so water companies deliver for customers and the environment."

articles.title: An Ohio family says its newly built luxury home arrived months late with about 40 defects, prompting $37,275 to be held in escrow; November 25 appeals judges revived their claims against the builder
articles.summary: An Ohio family’s dispute over a newly built luxury home has been revived by the state’s First District Court of Appeals, giving them another chance to
articles.body: An Ohio family’s dispute over a newly built luxury home has been revived by the state’s First District Court of Appeals, giving them another chance to pursue claims against the builder. According to the appellate opinion, the DeLaets allege that Sterling Homes delayed construction for several months and delivered a home with roughly 40 defects identified during a final walkthrough. Rather than delay closing, the parties agreed to hold $37,275 in escrow while the builder addressed more significant structural problems. On November 25, the appeals court reversed a trial court’s partial summary judgment for Sterling Homes and sent the case back for further proceedings, as per details on Justia U.S. Law.The ruling does not decide whether the builder was negligent, whether the repairs were completed, or how much money the family may ultimately recover. Instead, it restores the family’s opportunity to develop and present evidence supporting their allegations. The court found that Sterling Homes had not met its initial burden when it sought summary judgment, because it did not provide adequate record evidence to show that the family could not prove financial damages. Read more details about it here:What the family allegesThe case, Sarasota Beach House Trust v. Sterling Homes, L.L.C., was filed in January 2023 by the Sarasota Beach House Trust and trustees Edward L. DeLaet, Rebecca Kravitz DeLaet, and David DeLaet. Their complaint says Sterling Homes was responsible for constructing their new luxury home and that the project was delayed for several months before delivery. During a final walkthrough with Sterling’s property manager, the family says they identified approximately 40 items requiring repair.Rather than postpone the closing, the parties entered into an escrow arrangement involving $37,275. The stated purpose was to ensure that money would be available while Sterling addressed the more significant structural problems in the home. The DeLaets allege that, when they filed their lawsuit, many necessary repairs still had not been made.Their complaint raised four claims: breach of the construction contract, breach of the escrow agreement, violation of Ohio’s Home Construction Service Suppliers Act, and violation of the Consumer Sales Practices Act. They sought monetary damages and attorney fees. Sterling Homes denied the allegations in part and filed counterclaims alleging that it had substantially completed the repairs covered by the escrow agreement.Why the case was revivedThe appeal centered on a procedural question: could Sterling obtain partial summary judgment simply by arguing that the DeLaets had no evidence of financial damage? The appellate court said no. Under Ohio’s civil rules, the party seeking summary judgment must first identify record evidence showing that no genuine dispute exists on an essential element of the claim. A bare assertion that the other side lacks proof is not enough.Sterling argued that the DeLaets had failed to respond to discovery requests and therefore could not prove damages. But the appeals court found that Sterling had not submitted affidavits, transcripts, pleadings, admissions, or other qualifying evidence to establish that claim. The only document Sterling submitted was an unauthenticated blank copy of its discovery requests, which the court said did not meet the evidentiary standard for summary judgment.The court also rejected the idea that an alleged failure to respond to discovery, by itself, proved that the DeLaets suffered no damages. Even if the family had been late in responding, the court said, that would show dilatory communication, not the absence of financial harm. The court further noted that discovery sanctions generally require a court order compelling discovery, and no such order had been issued in this case.Leaks and claimed lossesThe DeLaets described two significant leaks at the home during the summer of 2024. In affidavits, they attributed one leak to improper bathroom tiling and another to incorrectly sealed pipes inside a wall. They also stated that their financial damages exceeded $40,000, although the appellate court observed that the affidavits contained only a conclusory statement on that point.Later, in seeking reconsideration of the trial court’s ruling, the family submitted repair estimates and invoices intended to document the amount of their claimed losses. Sterling argued that those materials were created and disclosed after the discovery deadline and asked the trial court to strike them. The trial court denied both Sterling’s motion to strike and the family’s request for reconsideration.Those damages documents were not the basis of the appellate court’s decision. The appeals court reversed the earlier ruling because Sterling had failed to carry its initial evidentiary burden, not because it found the invoices or estimates sufficient to prove the family’s case. The family will still need to prove its damages and the other elements of its claims as the case moves forward.What happens nextThe appellate court reversed the trial court’s judgment and remanded the case to the Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas for further proceedings. That means the DeLaets’ claims are once again live, and the parties can continue discovery, address evidentiary issues, and potentially proceed toward trial if the dispute is not resolved earlier. The court made clear that the trial judge may manage evidence and party conduct under Ohio’s civil rules on remand.The decision also acknowledges concerns about the family’s litigation conduct. The appellate panel noted that the DeLaets sought a discovery extension after the deadline had passed, submitted summary judgment responses that did not directly address damages, and waited until reconsideration to present invoices and estimates. The court said those actions do not limit the trial court’s authority to impose appropriate case-management measures.For homeowners, the case is a reminder that construction disputes often turn on documentation. Walkthrough lists, photographs, contractor communications, repair invoices, expert reports, and a clearly written escrow agreement can all matter when parties disagree about whether work was completed properly. For builders, the ruling underscores that a summary judgment motion requires more than an argument that the opposing party has not yet produced proof.The broader takeawayThe appellate ruling is significant because it reinforces a basic protection in civil litigation: a defendant cannot avoid a claim merely by saying the plaintiff has no evidence. The moving party must point to admissible record evidence and show why summary judgment is warranted. In this dispute, the court concluded that Sterling had not done so.That does not guarantee a win for the DeLaets. It simply means their allegations, including the claimed construction delays, the roughly 40 walkthrough defects, and the $37,275 escrow arrangement, will receive further consideration in the trial court. The ultimate question of whether Sterling breached its obligations, completed the required repairs, or caused compensable damage remains open.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: At 43, a former finance worker quit, sold her house and travelled Europe; she returned as a search-and-rescue ranger at Arizona’s Grand Canyon
articles.summary: Discover how Emily left her corporate finance job to become a Search-and-Rescue Ranger at Arizona's Grand Canyon, showcasing the transformative power of following your passion.
articles.body: According to the National Park Service's Behind the Scenery podcast, Emily was 43 when she recorded her episode. By then, she had built a career in finance and talent management, earned two master's degrees and completed dozens of marathons, but years earlier she had decided to leave her corporate life behind, sell her house and travel through Europe. Her journey eventually brought her to Arizona's Grand Canyon, where she found a new career as a Preventive Search and Rescue Ranger. Emily shared her story in the National Park Service's Behind the Scenery podcast episode, We Are the Rangers (and Friends). She told the podcast she had arrived at the North Rim in 2017, after a career in finance and talent management.Leaving finance to travel EuropePrior to joining the National Park Service, Emily was a certified public accountant and then moved into talent management and leadership development. She also obtained a master’s degree in organisational development. According to the host of the podcast, Emily had one bachelor’s degree and two master’s degrees. The reason behind Emily leaving her career path came from her difficult experience in her personal life because her mother was ill and Emily wanted to take a break from her busy schedule. As she stated, it was time to appreciate the time in her life. Emily left her job, sold her house and purchased a plane ticket to Europe to travel for around 12 months with the money that she saved before. She was planning to go back to the USA, select another city and obtain employment in the same field. When Emily returned to the US, she moved to an Airstream trailer in Tucson and worked as an accountant. After this employment opportunity finished, she received an email about a seasonal position in the Grand Canyon by the Grand Canyon Conservancy.Finding a new direction at the Grand CanyonThis seasonal position entailed working at the North Rim Visitor Centre and accommodation in the form of her own recreational vehicle. The salary was modest, but Emily was happy to have the chance to live within a national park. Initially, she intended to work for just eight weeks at the end of the season. During the period, she met the interpretive rangers and worked and cycled on the trails. Being an Ironman triathlete at that point, she also ran on the trails and hiked through the canyon. This inspired her to pursue her career as a ranger. As she had no prior professional experience in outdoor conservation or trail maintenance, she volunteered as part of a trail crew the winter after this. She later worked at Yosemite National Park and spent seasons doing field operations.Building the skill for search and rescueEmily got certified as an emergency medical technician because she wished to work in faraway places. In winter 2020-2021, Emily was offered employment as an interpreter in a place called Phantom Ranch in the Grand Canyon. The job meant a 14-mile hike down one week and back out the next. Working in this place, Emily developed an interest in emergencies as well as search and rescue calls. Later, she went through training in fighting fires and got an advanced certification as an EMT. She managed to take steps towards emergency services at the North Rim because of these certifications.At the time of the interview, Emily was a Preventive Search and Rescue Ranger. Among her responsibilities, Emily mentioned helping people on the trail, riding mountain bikes and helping with emergencies. Emily was also involved with ambulances and fire engines in the developed area. It took Emily five years of careful preparation to get into the ranger position. For her, it was hard to start over again after many years of working in the private sector, but Emily considered her ranger position to be her dream job. Her experience shows how a major career change can involve several smaller steps. For Emily, leaving finance was only the beginning. Volunteering and seasonal jobs further training helped her build a new working life at the Grand Canyon.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will convene his security cabinet on Thursday evening amid heightened tensions with Iran and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will convene his security cabinet on Thursday evening amid heightened tensions with Iran and preparations by Israel and the United States for a possible military operation against Tehran, Times of Israel reported.The meeting comes as Israel remains on alert over warnings that Iran could launch a surprise attack. It also follows a series of increasingly hardline statements from Iranian officials, including threats to disrupt oil exports across the region if Tehran is prevented from selling its own oil.The office of an Israeli government minister confirmed the planned meeting to The Times of Israel, which first reported the development.Israel's military has said it is prepared to strike Iran even without American support. Military spokesman Effie Defrin told Israeli public broadcaster Kan on Thursday that the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) was ready to act independently if required.“We are monitoring the situation and are ready to strike with force at any moment, including on our own, without the Americans,” Defrin said.Asked about the tensions with Tehran, he said, “There is no change in the guidelines. Iran’s vision of destroying Israel has not faded. They are working toward that goal.”Iran threatens regional oil exportsThe latest escalation comes as Iran has threatened to widen the economic and security consequences of the confrontation, particularly around the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.Iranian deputy parliament speaker Hamidreza Hajibabaei said on Thursday that Tehran would prevent oil exports from across the region if its own exports were blocked.“If Iran’s oil is not exported, no oil will leave the region,” Hajibabaei said.He warned that countries in the region assisting the United States in the Strait of Hormuz or elsewhere in the Persian Gulf could face retaliation. “The Islamic Republic will target that entire area,” he said.Hajibabaei also described attempts to export oil by bypassing the Strait of Hormuz as “a legitimate target” if they were intended to help the United States and Europe by bringing down oil prices.“Anyone who takes such action to help the US economically is at war with the Islamic Republic,” he said.The deputy speaker also suggested that Tehran could revise its military approach. “If necessary, we will change our defense doctrine,” he said.“In the event of any new aggression, we will use all legitimate means and capabilities at our disposal to strike our enemies anywhere in the world,” he added.Tensions raise concerns over wider regional conflictThe developments come amid growing concerns over the security of energy infrastructure and maritime routes in the region.Oil prices have risen amid reports of attacks and threats to shipping. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have claimed an attack on Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery, while Iranian media reported that two oil tankers struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The claims have not been independently verified.The United States has also stepped up economic pressure on Tehran through Operation Economic Outcast, launched by the US Treasury in August to restrict Iran's oil revenues.Meanwhile, Washington has held discussions with Gulf Cooperation Council countries and Jordan on regional security and efforts to increase pressure on Iran.The developments have added to concerns that any direct military confrontation between Israel and Iran could extend beyond the two countries, threatening energy supplies and shipping routes across the Gulf.Netanyahu's security cabinet meeting is taking place against this backdrop. articles.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
articles.summary: A landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) convicted Myanmar of genocide against its Rohingya minority.
articles.body:
Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.

The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.

Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.

"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.

The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.

The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.

The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.

The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.

The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.

The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.

But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.

While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.

More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders .

Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.

Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

articles.title: Private dentists too expensive for millions, watchdog warns
articles.summary: The Competitions and Market Authority says reforms are needed to make sure people get a fair deal.
articles.body:
The Competition watchdog says wide-ranging reforms are needed in the UK's private dentistry market to ensure people get a fair deal.

It says patients can struggle with costs and find it difficult to shop around and compare prices.

Around four million people did not go to the dentist in the past two years because they found treatment expensive, the watchdog estimates.

The British Dental Association says it is essential that there is a thriving private market but it is also vital that the government fixes NHS dentistry.

The Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) interim report on private dentist services says millions of people are struggling with the costs of private dental care, with some delaying or going without treatment.

Private dentist services are now used by about 60% of UK patients for some care

At large dental groups prices rose by around 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025, ahead of inflation and wage increases

A composite white filling is equivalent to about 36% of average weekly disposable income in the North East of England and 35% in Wales

There is wide variation in prices even in the same local area. In Preston, composite fillings ranged from £80 to £223

An amalgam filling (sometimes known as a silver filling) costs anything between £72 and £159 in Caerphilly

Lisa Frame, aged 64, from Norfolk, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that while her private treatment was very good, she felt resentful about the overall costs.

She needed three extractions, and a temporary and then permanent plate, costing around £2600.

"I am a retired lady but I do not receive a pension until I'm 67 and I have had to rely on my husband to help me.

"The dentist I have…has given a first class service but I still feel very resentful that I'd have had to pay so much money when I have made NHS contributions all my working life," she said.

Why is it so hard to find an NHS dentist? Find out how many have closed where you live

The report argues it is difficult for patients to shop around for a good deal, with one in six practices in the UK not publishing prices online.

The watchdog also says private dentists can have financial incentives to promote treatments and this can create a risk that patients are sold services not in their best interests.

There is also evidence that some practices have targets to switch NHS patients to private care.

The CMA says there can be substantial variation in profit margins between practices.

Underlying many of these issues is a shortage of dentists.

The UK has fewer dentists per person in the population than most European countries, with a high vacancy rate in practices and that can hold back the expansion of services.

The market isn't working well for dental patients according to Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA.

"Many people are struggling with affordability, and those on lower incomes and in certain parts of the UK are hardest hit," she said.

"We're proposing a wide-ranging package of measures to change the way the market operates and will work with governments across the UK to finalise these recommendations ahead of our final report in March."

The British Dental Association (BDA) said it would work with the competition watchdog to come up with practical measures but said governments in the UK should make fundamental reforms to NHS dentistry.

Eddie Crouch, chair of the BDA, said: "It is essential that we have a thriving private dental market.

"But successive governments have left millions with no options when it comes to securing NHS care.

"When it comes to giving patients access to affordable care ministers hold almost all the cards."

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday finally broke silence on Imran Masood's aggressive attack on Samajwadi Party over
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday finally broke silence on Imran Masood's aggressive attack on Samajwadi Party over seat-sharing in Uttar Pradesh.Speaking at an event in Lucknow, Kharge advised Masood to "focus on action rather than just words", as the Saharanpur MP's increasingly sharp remarks against ally Samajwadi Party (SP) have added to the strain over seat-sharing negotiations ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections."... Imran Masood — whom I frequently hear on television, where he often speaks with great passion. However, we must focus on action rather than just words; the more we work together, the further we will progress. He is in Parliament, where he consistently fights for the party and strives to ensure that our positions are upheld," Kharge said.The Congress chief's remarks come amid growing friction between the two INDIA bloc allies, with Masood repeatedly questioning the SP's approach to seat-sharing even as discussions between the parties remain under way.Masood questions SP's seat-sharing approachMasood on Thursday questioned the rationale behind continuing seat-sharing discussions after the Akhilesh Yadav-led SP announced five candidates while negotiations with the Congress were still in progress."It is no alliance if one partner 'leaves' seats for the other after announcing its candidates," he said, raising questions about whether the Congress was being treated as an equal partner.The Congress MP also made it clear that he would remain with his party and would not accept a subordinate position in the alliance."What else should I say? You (SP) release the list. Then you leave the seats. Are we alliance partners or your servants? Did we ask you to leave these seats for us? We had discussed the matter, and now an order has been issued that we should not speak about those discussions," he said.Masood, who was involved in the seat-sharing discussions, argued that an alliance should involve joint decisions and announcements. He declined to comment on the SP's manifesto, which was scheduled to be released later on Thursday, saying he was unaware of the party's approach."It is their decision. How can I comment on it? The meaning of an alliance is that there should be joint press conferences and everything should be joint. If something else is happening here, I do not know about it," he said.Recalling the previous Assembly elections contested by the Congress and SP, Masood said his party had fought 107 seats when Akhilesh Yadav was the chief minister of Uttar Pradesh."Now, he is yet to become the chief minister," he added.Earlier barbs had put SP on the defensiveMasood's latest remarks follow a series of public attacks on the SP leadership over the alliance arrangement. On Wednesday, he had used sharp expressions to convey his frustration with what he described as the SP's treatment of the Congress.In an interview with The Times of India, he questioned whether the SP wanted to fight the BJP or its own alliance partner."Aapki ladai mujhe samajh nahi aa rahi hai — BJP se ladni hai ya humse? Aap hamare gale par pair rakhkar, hamari kabar ke upar Taj Mahal banana chahenge, toh mera saans ghutega. Main toh haath-pair maarunga (I am unable to understand your battle … You want to fight the BJP or us. If you will want to stand on my neck and build a Taj Mahal on my grave, I will be suffocated. I will fight back)," he had said.Later, speaking to a television channel, Masood compared the Congress to zero, arguing that its presence multiplied the strength of an alliance partner by ten."If you don't understand our importance, then OK, Goodbye, Thank You," he said.The SP had largely refrained from responding to his remarks throughout Wednesday. However, his repeated criticism prompted some SP functionaries to question the Congress leadership's silence.A senior SP functionary told TOI that either the Congress leadership was choosing to ignore the statements or was unaware of what its leaders were saying. Neither possibility, he suggested, was a positive sign for the alliance.The functionary also pointed out that Masood and AICC's Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam had previously targeted the SP leadership over the alliance, but SP leaders had avoided responding following instructions from party chief Akhilesh Yadav not to comment publicly on seat-sharing discussions.The SP's concern, according to the functionary, was not merely that Congress leaders were criticising the party, but that the Congress leadership had not publicly objected to what it considered unprovoked remarks.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Dublin M50: Three more youths charged over wrong-way collision
articles.summary: Seven youths in total have now been charged in connection with a crash in which a man in his 20s was seriously injured.
articles.body:
Three more youths have been charged in connection with a crash on Dublin's M50 in which a man in his 20s was seriously injured.

A vehicle travelling the wrong way collided head-on with his car near junction 12 at Firhouse on 9 August.

Gardaí (Irish police) said three youths arrested as part of the investigation have been charged and will appear before court in Dublin on Thursday.

Four youths appeared at a late court sitting in Dublin on Wednesday, charged in connection with the incident.

Gardaí said the vehicle was travelling north on the motorway's southbound carriageway and was driving down an entry slip road when the collision happened.

They said they remain in contact with the injured driver and have made him aware of developments in the investigation.

articles.title: Seven injured, four critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
articles.summary: Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as officials urged residents to leave the area.
articles.body:
Seven people have been injured - four of them critically - after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, local government officials have said.

A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).

The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.

Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.

A alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.

Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.

The city-run Erawan Emergency Medical Centre said it was treating four "red" cases and three "yellow" - less severe - cases.

On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.

He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.

Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.

It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.

An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

articles.title: Veruschka: Striking images of one of the world's first supermodels, who has died aged 87
articles.summary: Veruschka was a model and artist who became one of one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s.
articles.body:
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.

She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."

She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.

Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.

Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.

She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute .

"She worked with Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, and Valentino, but also immersed herself in avant-garde photography projects in which she painted, staged, and deconstructed her body.

"Veruschka was never just a model – she was an artist, a boundary-pusher, a rebel. Her work is considered a feminist precursor to performance art."

articles.title: Lenacapavir: Uganda and Zambia lead rollout of low-cost HIV prevention jab
articles.summary: Lenacapavir, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection.
articles.body:
Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.

The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.

The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.

Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.

The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.

The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.

Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering new hope for HIV prevention?

Landmark deal paves way for cheaper HIV protection jab

Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.

In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.

Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025 .

The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.

More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.

The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.

It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.

Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.

South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.

Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.

The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

articles.title: Coventry-born NHS psychiatrist swaps consulting room for cinema
articles.summary: Parvinder Shergill wrote, directed and stars in the fencing drama, shown in Coventry on Friday.
articles.body:
An NHS psychiatrist who taught herself filmmaking is bringing her first cinema release to her home city.

Dr Parvinder Shergill's film Touché, which explores mental health through the sport of fencing, will be screened at Coventry's Odeon on Friday.

The Coventry-born consultant psychiatrist, who works in London, wrote and directed the film and stars alongside Matthew Lewis, Nina Wadia and Paul Chowdhry, with Sir Stephen Fry narrating.

Shergill said her passion for cinema began when her father, who still lives in her home city, introduced her to Steven Spielberg's films at the age of four.

However, her route into the film industry was not a conventional one.

"I'm British Indian. It's a stereotype, but my parents were like, 'you've got to be a doctor'," she said.

"So I was like, 'OK, if I get the degree, can I do film after?'

"They were like, 'yeah, yes'. And I held them to it."

Since starting her film and television career in 2020, Shergill has appeared in Coronation Street and Emmerdale, as well as writing, producing and directing her own material.

Touché, her fifth film as a director, tells the story of Deep, a British South Asian woman who finds a sense of community through fencing.

"I've always wanted to tell a fencing film, I always say it's like Karate Kid meets fencing with a girl," she said.

Community 'heartbroken' after fire destroys historic club

'City's masked e-bike riders intimidate us'

Archers fans urged to back fight to keep show in city

Shergill believes the film's mental health message was what attracted Fry to the project.

She said her work as a psychiatrist influenced her storytelling and themes of mental health could be found even in superhero films.

"I naturally, consciously and unconsciously, thread through mental health specifically in my work because I think even DC [and] Marvel superhero films, the hero always has some sort of fall, low mood or anxiety and they've got to rise back up and save the day," she explained.

"It's actually in everything we watch, we just don't realize it."

She said she wanted to see the two industries in which she worked learn from each other.

"I want the NHS to be more creative and I want the creative industry to be a bit more sort of safeguarding with doctors as well."

Despite juggling two careers, Shergill said her enthusiasm for filmmaking had never diminished.

"It's a bit cliche, but it is sort of my soulmate. I live and breathe it.

"It's a bit pathetic. I wake up and just think about creativity and that's all you can do.

articles.title: Heathrow Airport third runway plans 'should be grounded'
articles.summary: The runway plans do not fully address issues including climate tests, the Transport Committee says.
articles.body:
The government has "failed to make the case" for Heathrow Airport's expansion, the chair of the Transport Committee has said, as a highly anticipated report on the £33bn project is published.

Ruth Cadbury said the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement did not adequately address noise, air pollution and climate tests.

"Plans for a third runway should be grounded for now and the government should go back to the drawing board," she said.

Downing Street has repeatedly said the prime minister would wait for the Transport Committee's report, among other factors, before deciding whether to back the scheme. The prime minister's office has been contacted for comment.

What's the plan for a third runway at Heathrow Airport?

The report said the climate test was examined in the context of the recent advice from the Climate Change Committee.

The results showed the west London airport's expansion would not be compatible with the UK's carbon budgets or net-zero targets, it said.

The committee said both the air quality test and the noise test should be strengthened, adding that there was a lack of certainty over the cost of expansion that could affect the prices paid by airlines and passengers.

It also raised concerns over a lack of extensive plans to improve public transport, such as new rail lines into Heathrow from the west and south.

"If a third runway is to get off the ground, then government also needs to strengthen the air quality test and noise tests, develop plans for improving public transport and bottom out how much it will cost airlines and passengers to use an expanded Heathrow," Cadbury said.

She also called for "robust analysis" to set out what would happen if decarbonisation goals were missed.

"Expansion should not go ahead at any price, or at any cost to society or the environment," the report said.

A spokesperson for the Department for Transport said the government had made clear that Heathrow expansion could only go ahead if it met four tests covering economic growth, climate change, noise and air quality.

They added: "We note the findings from the committee's report and will consider these as we continue to review responses to our consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion."

Paul McGuinness, chair of the No 3rd Runway Coalition group, said the expansion would "leave the country worse off, once the negative costs are taken into account".

However, Heathrow's chief executive Thomas Woldbye said the "overwhelming weight of evidence and support remains strongly behind Heathrow expansion".

"Successive governments, independent commissions and industry experts have repeatedly concluded that you either expand Heathrow so the UK can compete and grow, or you accept a steady erosion of the UK's connectivity and global competitiveness," he said.

Cadbury, Labour MP for Brentford and Isleworth in west London, has been outspoken about her opposition to the expansion .

Lord Khan, who was the MP for Tooting before becoming London mayor in 2016, also opposes a third runway .

He previously told BBC Radio London that noise, air pollution and climate change targets were his main concerns.

Then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced last year the government was backing the scheme .

She previously said it would add 0.5% to the UK's GDP, although updated government forecasts in June recalibrated this figure at just 0.05%.

The Transport Committee's report said the government had positioned expansion as "critical" to national growth, but that "the case for this designation applying to Heathrow expansion has not been made".

Heathrow is the UK's busiest airport, serving more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways.

The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average - if a third runway is built.

It is estimated the project would create 100,000 jobs.

But it would see homes demolished, rivers diverted and the M25 motorway rerouted through a tunnel between junctions 14 and 15.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested a date of 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

articles.title: Accredited vs self-proclaimed: SC to examine protection for journalists
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday referred allegations of police assault, manhandling and wrongful detention of seven journalists covering protests
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday referred allegations of police assault, manhandling and wrongful detention of seven journalists covering protests in Delhi in October to a high-powered inquiry committee headed by former Supreme Court judge Justice R Subhash Reddy.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the petitioners to submit relevant material before the five-member committee, which will examine the allegations and establish whether the journalists were subjected to police excesses.The petitions were filed by the Kerala Union of Working Journalists (KUWJ) and the Delhi Union of Journalists over alleged police action against media personnel covering protests on October 10 and 11, 2026. The demonstrations were reportedly demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.Justice Bagchi said the committee would ascertain whether the journalists were present at the protest sites, whether force was used against them and, if so, whether it was excessive in the circumstances."You will go back to the committee which we have constituted to factually demonstrate whether your petitioners were, in fact, present there. If present, whether they were subjected to excessive force," he observed, as quoted by PTI.The judge added that the committee should examine whether the force used was disproportionate to what was necessary for maintaining public order.The bench also indicated that it would consider broader constitutional questions concerning the protection available to journalists covering protests and public events, including whether accredited journalists are entitled to greater protection than self-proclaimed reporters.Justice Bagchi observed that self-proclaimed journalists may not enjoy the same protection as accredited media persons.Appearing for the journalists, senior advocate PV Dinesh said the seven media personnel worked for established news organisations and were not social media reel-makers."We are just journalists, recognised journalists. Allow us to do our work," he submitted.He also questioned whether journalists working for established media organisations could be taken into custody while performing their professional duties."The question is, when established journalists, who are recognised journalists, are covering events, can they be taken into custody?" Dinesh asked, as quoted by PTI.The court indicated that it would examine the constitutional safeguards available to journalists, including their freedom of movement and right to practise their profession. It would also consider whether forcibly removing a journalist from a location amounts to custody and the legal consequences of such action.The petitioners alleged that journalists were forcibly removed from reporting locations, prevented from recording events and subjected to physical force despite displaying their press credentials. The allegations also include an attempt to snatch a photographer's camera and the physical assault of a woman journalist while she was reporting live.The seven journalists named in the petition are Suhail Muhammed and VS Rahul of 24 News, Sajin of Asianet News, Roshni Rajan and Farsana of Reporter TV, Vishnuprasad of Mathrubhumi and Miji P Jose of Manorama News.The Delhi Police had earlier told the Supreme Court that social media influencers and reel-makers cannot claim the same protections as journalists covering protests.In an affidavit, the police described journalists as a "distinct category" from social media content creators who use cameras and microphones to make reels for commercial gain.
