articles.title: Government's antisemitism adviser launches investigation into BBC
articles.summary: Lord Mann says he has launched the investigation after "growing discomfort among Jewish BBC staff".
articles.body:
The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.

Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".

He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."

The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".

The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".

The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".

Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019 , said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".

"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".

"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.

"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."

The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.

He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".

His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".

Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".

He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".

He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS , which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.

The Guardian recently reported that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.

"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.

"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.

"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."

The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.

"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.

"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."

Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.

The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.

In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".

Last September, the BBC's broadcast of Bob Vylan's controversial set at Glastonbury broke editorial guidelines in relation to harm and offence , with the corporation's complaints unit ruling that some comments could "fairly be characterised as antisemitic". The band denied being antisemitic.

articles.title: Five people never returned from a Titanic expedition in 2023; more than $50 million lawsuit filed by French explorer Paul-Henri Nargeolet's estate questions OceanGate's safety decisions and the construction of its doomed submersible
articles.summary: The Titan submersible implosion in June 2023 killed five people during an expedition to the wreckage of the Titanic, raising questions about the vessel's
articles.body: The Titan submersible implosion in June 2023 killed five people during an expedition to the wreckage of the Titanic, raising questions about the vessel's construction, safety systems and the decisions made before its final voyage. Among those who died was French deep-sea explorer Paul-Henri Nargeolet, who had spent decades visiting the wreck. In August 2024, Richard Ortoli, administrator of Nargeolet's estate, filed a wrongful-death lawsuit seeking more than $50 million from OceanGate and five other defendants. The complaint accused those involved in designing, building and operating Titan of gross negligence and alleged that safety concerns had not been adequately addressed before its final dive.French explorer’s estate raises questions over Titan's construction and safetyThe complaint was filed in King County Superior Court in Washington on August 6, 2024. It named OceanGate, the estate of its late chief executive Stockton Rush, former engineering director Tony Nissen and three other companies as defendants. The estate accused them of gross negligence in connection with Titan's design, construction and operation.The estate alleged that the submersible had been developed and operated outside established practices in the deep-sea diving industry. Particular concerns were raised about its carbon-fibre pressure hull and the use of materials and components that differed from those found in conventional deep-diving vessels.The complaint also questioned Rush's approach to the project, alleging that his desire to establish himself as an innovator in underwater exploration had taken precedence over accepted safety practices. It claimed that the company had ignored warnings about the vessel and failed to adequately address concerns surrounding its construction.These accusations formed part of the estate's case and were allegations rather than judicial findings of negligence when the lawsuit was filed. The complaint sought damages exceeding $50 million, including compensation for losses associated with Nargeolet's death and claims relating to the suffering allegedly experienced before the implosion.Lawsuit raises questions about passengers' final momentsOne of the more significant allegations concerned what the five occupants may have known before Titan imploded. The estate alleged that Titan's acoustic monitoring system was capable of detecting unusual cracking sounds from the carbon-fibre hull as the vessel came under extreme pressure. According to the complaint, such sounds could have indicated that the pressure vessel was experiencing structural problems.According to the complaint, the system was designed to identify unusual sounds that could indicate structural problems. The estate argued that such warnings could have alerted the pilot to the developing danger and prompted an attempt to abort the descent.The filing also alleged that the people inside Titan may have realised the vessel was failing before the implosion. It claimed they could have experienced fear and mental anguish during those final moments.However, the suggestion that the passengers knew they were facing imminent death was not established by the investigation. In June 2024, Marine Board of Investigation chairman Captain Jason Neubauer told The New York Times that investigators had found no evidence that the occupants were aware of their impending fate.Why the lawsuit questioned Titan's constructionNargeolet's estate argued that the explorer had been aware that Titan differed from other submersibles, including its use of carbon fibre in the pressure hull. However, the complaint pointed out that he was not an engineer, physicist or specialist in submersible design. It suggested that he had relied on assurances from Rush about the vessel's safety and seaworthiness. The estate argued that Nargeolet had not been given a complete understanding of the risks associated with its construction and operation.The complaint also referred to concerns raised by specialists before the final expedition. Questions had been raised about whether the vessel's design could withstand repeated exposure to the pressures encountered during deep-sea dives. The legal filing alleged that important information about Titan's limitations and potential safety problems had not been adequately disclosed. It also questioned whether the company had taken appropriate steps to address warnings about the vessel before allowing it to continue operating.Nargeolet had completed 37 dives to the Titanic wreckKnown as 'Mr Titanic', Nargeolet had a long association with the famous shipwreck. He served as director of underwater research at RMS Titanic, the company that holds the salvage rights to the wreck. According to Fortune, his involvement with the site began in 1987, shortly after the Titanic's location was discovered shortly after the Titanic's location was discovered. Over the years, he participated in 37 dives to the wreck, becoming one of the most experienced explorers associated with underwater expeditions to the site.His experience was also an important part of the estate's argument. The complaint suggested that someone with Nargeolet's background would not have agreed to take part in the expedition had he been fully informed about the alleged problems with Titan. The estate maintained that his familiarity with deep-sea exploration should not be confused with specialist knowledge of pressure-vessel engineering. It argued that he had placed his trust in the assurances provided by the company and its chief executive.Five people died when Titan imploded in June 2023The disaster occurred on June 18, 2023, during a descent towards the Titanic wreck in the North Atlantic. The submersible lost contact with its support vessel, prompting a search and rescue operation that continued for several days. The US Coast Guard later confirmed that debris from Titan had been found on the ocean floor, establishing that the vessel had suffered a catastrophic implosion. All five people aboard were killed.Alongside Nargeolet and Rush, those on the expedition included British businessman and adventurer Hamish Harding, Pakistani businessman Shahzada Dawood and his 19-year-old son, Suleman Dawood. The incident brought renewed attention to questions about the safety of privately operated deep-sea submersibles. Titan's unconventional construction, its testing procedures and the extent of independent scrutiny before its commercial expeditions became subjects of wider concern.OceanGate suspended its exploration and commercial operations following the disaster.What US and Canadian investigators found about OceanGate's safety failuresThe US Coast Guard's Marine Board of Investigation released its final report on August 5, 2025, identifying several factors that contributed to the Titan disaster. Investigators concluded that OceanGate's inadequate design, certification, maintenance and inspection procedures played a significant role in the implosion. The investigation also found that the company had failed to properly investigate and address known anomalies in Titan's pressure hull following its 2022 expedition. Data collected by the vessel's real-time monitoring system should have been analysed and acted upon, but OceanGate failed to take appropriate action.In October 2025, the National Transportation Safety Board published its own findings, identifying OceanGate's inadequate engineering process as the probable cause of the implosion. Investigators concluded that the company had failed to establish the actual strength and durability of Titan's pressure vessel. The report also identified delamination damage in the carbon-fibre structure, which was worsened by additional damage and eventually led to a local buckling failure.Canada's Transportation Safety Board also published its final investigation report on June 17, 2026. Its findings highlighted deficiencies in OceanGate's risk management and the testing of Titan's acoustic monitoring system, alongside gaps in the oversight of privately operated submersibles.Lawsuit filed by Nargeolet's estateThe lawsuit also underwent a procedural change in January 2025, when a federal judge ordered the case to be returned to King County Superior Court in Washington. The decision addressed where the proceedings should take place and did not determine whether the defendants were liable for Nargeolet's death. Nargeolet's lawyers said the case was intended to establish how the disaster occurred, who was involved and whether those responsible had allowed Titan to operate despite potential safety concerns. Attorney Tony Buzbee said the family wanted answers about the circumstances surrounding the implosion. An OceanGate spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit, according to Associated Press.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: William Dunlop recommended for release by Parole Board
articles.summary: William Dunlop, who strangled Julie Hogg in County Durham, was jailed after a double jeopardy law change.
articles.body:
A murderer who became the first person tried after a change to the 800-year-old double jeopardy law has been recommended for release from prison.

William Dunlop, now 63, strangled Julie Hogg, 22, in Billingham, County Durham, in 1989 and hid her mutilated body behind a bath panel which was discovered by her mother more than two months later.

The Parole Board has recommended he be released after his fourth application to review his case. A panel had recommended Dunlop's transfer to open prison multiple times but three justice secretaries had intervened.

In response to the result, Hogg's son Kevin called the Parole Board "not fit for purpose".

The 22-year-old's murder was "accompanied by the brutal sexual degradation of [her] body", the Old Bailey judge said at Dunlop's sentencing, which came in 2006 after Julie Hogg's family campaigned for the legal change so he could be charged with the same crime twice.

Kevin Hogg said: "You know them victim personal statements? They mean absolutely nothing – nothing whatsoever and that's been proven time and time again."

In its decision, the Parole Board concluded there was "no more than a minimal risk" Dunlop would go on to commit a further offence which would cause serious harm.

"After the time he has spent in custody and process of rehabilitation he has steadfastly pursued would not, in the judgment of this experienced panel, undermine the confidence of the public in the parole system," the decision read.

The panel said it was "mindful of the feelings" of Julie Hogg's mother Ann Ming, who believed Dunlop should never be released.

"However, if a prisoner presents as a person who, on the totality of the evidence available to the Panel, meets the statutory test for release then the Panel is obliged by law to conclude that his release must be directed."

The Parole Board acknowledged that the Secretary of State may still seek to review the decision, adding: "However, the Panel has had the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses, and, in particular, WD [William Dunlop]."

Kevin Hogg said: "When will they actually listen and take note of what the ministers said? Take note of what victims and the victims' families are saying?"

In his victim impact statement, Kevin Hogg recounted his childhood trauma of "hearing screaming and shouting in the home with the pungent smell of my mother's decomposing body" as his grandmother found it.

"I can say categorically that time isn't the great healer it's purported to be," he said.

"As the years pass, the pain of losing my mother to this murder remains acute."

Dunlop, known as Billy, was tried twice for the murder but both juries failed to reach a verdict.

Three years later, while in jail for another crime, he confessed and admitted lying in court, boasting there was nothing anyone could do about it because of the double jeopardy rule in place at the time.

Hogg's family, including her mother, campaigned for 15 years to get the law changed and he became the first person to be tried under the new rules.

He admitted murder and was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years.

At the public parole hearing last month , Dunlop, who psychiatrists previously found had "psychopathic traits" and "severe personality problems", told the panel that he now empathises with the family after his son died last year.

"I get it now. I totally get it now," he said.

Per Dunlop's request to not be seen, he spoke with his back to the camera that was live-streaming from an unnamed prison to a room in London with Hogg's family inside.

The following day, Ming, 80, said she "wanted to scream" when hearing of his newfound empathy, adding: "I don't know how we kept it together."

At the hearing, Dunlop's prison offender manager said his ability to cope had improved.

She said she observed this last year as he navigated his son's death, then-justice secretary Shabana Mahmood's intervention to keep him in the prison, and the documenting of his case in ITV drama I Fought the Law.

Dunlop has served five years more than his minimum term for murder.

He was already imprisoned at the time of that sentence and has now been detained for about 28 years.

articles.title: A Louisiana father gave his farm and home to his brother in 2014 while keeping the right to live there for life; after he died, his younger children challenged the transfer, but an appeals court left it intact
articles.summary: A Louisiana father gave his farm and home to his brother, while keeping the right to live there for the rest of his life.
articles.body: A Louisiana father gave his farm and home to his brother, while keeping the right to live there for the rest of his life. An appeals court ruled he did not unlawfully give away all his assets, turning down a challenge from three of his younger children after his death. The Louisiana Court of Appeal, Third Circuit, upheld the transfer of the property in Sulphur, Louisiana, finding the children failed to prove their father lacked enough resources to support himself when he made the gift in 2014. The ruling came out on 25 November 2026 and involves the estate of Donald Michael Ackel Sr. He transferred the property to his brother, Alex Leo Ackel, also known as Dickie Ackel, while keeping a lifetime usufruct over it. A usufruct is a legal right to use someone else's property and enjoy its benefits. The legal fight focused on whether Donald gave away his entire estate without keeping enough property or income for basic living needs, which would go against Louisiana law. In its decision, the Third Circuit agreed with the lower court that Donald kept living on the property as his home and that evidence showed he got Social Security benefits, so his children did not prove grounds to cancel the transfer.How the property transfer took placeAccording to the court's opinion, Donald signed an act of donation on 8 October 2014, transferring the immovable property at 7211 Choupique Road in Sulphur to his brother. The deal made Dickie the property owner while Donald kept a lifetime usufruct, a legal right that let him keep using the property for the rest of his life. Dickie later transferred the property to Al Ackel Farms LLC on 26 January 2015, where Alex Ackel was the sole member and manager, and the company later gave Donald a lifetime right of use and habitation on 14 September 2016. Under this setup, Donald could keep living at the property even after ownership moved to his brother and then to the company. The fight started after Donald died on 28 November 2023, leaving behind 12 children from three marriages. His three youngest children, Kelli Ackel, Joseph Lane Ackel, and Justin Ackel, challenged the transfer, with Justin's mother, Mary Katherine Stevens, filing the case for him because he was a minor. The children argued the property gift cut down the inheritance set aside for them as forced heirs under Louisiana law. Forced heirs are close relatives who have a legal right to a share of an estate.Children challenged the inheritance arrangementsDonald signed a will on 22 June 2021, leaving his entire estate to his oldest son, Samuel Michael Ackel, and naming him independent executor. Samuel filed to probate the will on 24 January 2024, with estate papers listing three bank accounts with a combined $8,109.11 as Donald's assets when he died. The younger children then filed a petition on 13 August 2024 to reopen the succession case and challenge the earlier property transfer. They asked the court to shrink what they called a too-large gift, bring certain gifts back into the estate through a legal step called collation, remove Samuel as executor, and accused people of fraud. The children said the donated property was worth more than $500,000 and argued giving it to their uncle hurt their legally protected shares of the inheritance. Their main point used Article 1498 of the Louisiana Civil Code, which bars a person from giving away all their property without keeping enough to live on. The defendants pushed back against the challenge, arguing Donald got $400,000 in cash tied to the deal, kept the right to live on the property until he died, and had their property taxes, repairs, and upkeep covered for nearly 10 years.Trial court found he retained enough to live onThe case went to trial after both sides failed to win summary judgment in October 2025. On 9 December 2025, the trial court dismissed the children's claims, ruling they did not show Donald lacked enough resources to live on when he transferred the property. The lower court looked at proof that Donald got Social Security benefits and kept a home through his lifetime usufruct. Even though the exact monthly benefit amount was not proven, the court found enough proof that he got regular payments, and the trial judge also noted the children did not show how much Donald needed for living costs when he made the gift. In its written reasons, the trial court explained the usufruct gave Donald shelter while his Social Security money helped pay for other basic needs. The children appealed, arguing the trial judge wrongly set aside witness testimony and leaned on guesses from indirect clues. They also argued their father gave away the only valuable property he owned while having money troubles.Appeals court examined the $400,000 payment claimIn reviewing the case, the Third Circuit looked at Donald's money situation when he made the gift rather than focusing on what happened to his money in later years. The court said Article 1498 required the children to prove their father did not keep enough property or resources to support himself. It also looked at the defendants' claim that Donald got $400,000 in cash after signing the transfer papers. Dickie testified the money was paid after the paperwork was signed and said the setup aimed to keep his brother from paying taxes on a property sale. The court said that claimed payment could not show whether Donald kept enough resources when he made the gift. It noted the paper recorded an inter vivos donation, which means a gift made while the giver is still alive rather than a sale. The judges also said money supposedly paid after the deal was not part of Donald's money when he signed the gift, so the court did not use the claimed $400,000 payment to show he had enough money to live on.Lifetime right to remain in the home proved importantA big part of the appeal focused on the legal rights Donald kept after giving up ownership. The Third Circuit explained a usufruct is a recognized property right that lets someone use property owned by another person for a set time. Even without ownership, Donald's lifetime usufruct let him keep using the whole property without interference from his brother, and the judges noted the deal did not clearly give Donald the right to rent out the property for income, so his kept rights mostly tied to using it as his home. Dickie testified he made the deal so his brother could stay there for life, telling the court the goal was for Donald always to have a place to live and explaining he wanted him to be able to "take his last breath on earth in his home." The appeals court also looked at proof that Donald lived on the property until he died and did not try to rent it out, deciding the lifetime usufruct gave him shelter that directly helped him live. The court also looked at proof about Donald's farm gear, vehicles, and horses, noting testimony showed he had owned a tractor, a truck, two bushhogs, a lawnmower, and several horses, though there was not enough proof that these items held high financial value. Even so, the judges found proof of Social Security benefits, paired with his right to live on the property, backed the lower court's ruling.Appeals court leaves donation intactThe Third Circuit ruled the trial judge made fair findings from the evidence and found no factual mistake serious enough to overturn the ruling. The court stressed it was up to the children to prove their father gave away his property without keeping enough for basic needs, and found they did not meet that burden. So, it upheld the 9 December 2025 ruling that dismissed the claims against Alex Ackel and Al Ackel Farms LLC, while appeal costs were also charged to Kelli Ackel, Joseph Lane Ackel, and Mary Katherine Stevens, acting for Justin Ackel. The ruling leaves the 2014 property gift in place and rejects the younger children's effort to pull the farm and home back into their father's estate to claim inheritance shares. The ruling came in In re Succession of Donald Michael Ackel Sr., docket number CA-0026-0315, from the Louisiana Court of Appeal, Third Circuit.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Diana Award charity placed into administration after 27 years
articles.summary: The charity, set up in memory of the late Princess of Wales, says it confirmed the news with "heavy hearts".
articles.body:
The Prince of Wales has expressed his sadness after the Diana Award, set up in memory of his mother, was placed into administration.

Prince William thanked "everyone whose dedication and hard work helped" encourage thousands of young people "over so many years".

A statement on the Diana Award website said it was announcing the news with "heavy hearts", but independent advice had "made clear" it could "no longer continue to meet its obligations".

"We are proud to have shone a spotlight on a generation of young people," said the charity, which was founded 27 years ago to support their development.

Diana, Princess of Wales, died in a car crash in Paris in 1997.

More than 50,000 young people have received the award - which recognises outstanding contributions to social action and humanitarian efforts.

The charity said it had supported thousands more "through programmes to power the impact created by these inspirational young leaders on the lives of those around them".

It was created "to honour Diana, Princess of Wales and her belief that young people had the power to change their community, their country and the world", the charity added.

The Duke of Sussex has also supported the charity.

A statement on the Diana Award website said of the news: "This is not the outcome any of us wanted.

"We thank everyone who has supported this charity over the years and, above all, the young people whose achievements have always been at the heart of it.

"Their achievements matter, and nothing about today's decision changes that."
